title: Stable Partition for Predictable Branches
description:
You must answer the same threshold query 100 times on an array of 100,000 integers.

In the baseline, each pass scans the original random-order array. Because the branch `arr[i] > 128` is nearly 50/50 on random data, the bimodal branch predictor mispredicts often.

You may preprocess the array once before the 100 passes begin. Reorder the data so the hot branch becomes easy to predict, while keeping exactly the same values and final sum as the reference implementation.
prompt: Write `long solve(int *arr, int n)` to return the sum of all values greater than 128 over 100 full passes. You may do one up-front preprocessing step before the repeated scans.
expectedOutput: Return one 64-bit integer equal to the reference sum over all 100 passes.
constraints: You may preprocess the array once before the repeated queries
Must preserve all original values exactly
Output must equal the reference total across all 100 passes

examples.output: total sum of all values > 128 across 100 passes
examples.explanation: A stable partition such as "all values <= 128 first, then all values > 128" turns a nearly random branch into two long predictable runs.

title: Matrix Multiply — Cache Tiling
description:
Multiply two row-major 512×512 float matrices: `C = A × B`.

The baseline reads rows of `A` but walks down columns of `B`, which gives poor spatial locality and creates avoidable cache misses.

Rewrite the loop nest with blocking, transposition, or both so the inner loops read memory in a cache-friendly order.
prompt: Write `void solve(float *A, float *B, float *C)` to compute the exact product of two row-major 512×512 matrices while improving cache locality.
expectedOutput: After `solve` returns, `C` must contain the exact matrix product for the provided inputs.

examples.explanation: Accessing B by columns causes poor locality. Transpose B or tile the loops so both operands are consumed sequentially inside the inner loops.

title: Reduction Tree — Break Dependency Chains
description:
Sum 100,000 floating-point values.

The baseline uses one running accumulator, so every addition depends on the previous one. That long dependency chain prevents the out-of-order core from overlapping many adds.

Restructure the reduction to create independent work, for example with multiple accumulators and loop unrolling, while staying within the allowed floating-point tolerance.
prompt: Write `void solve(float *arr, float *out)` so `out[0]` becomes the sum of 100,000 floats, using a loop structure that exposes more instruction-level parallelism than a single running accumulator.
expectedOutput: `out[0]` must match the reference reduction within a tolerance of 1e-4.
constraints: Result must match the reference within fp tolerance 1e-4
You may unroll and reorder additions

examples.explanation: Several partial sums let the CPU work on multiple additions at once instead of waiting for one long dependency chain.

title: Pointer Chasing — Recover Memory Parallelism
description:
You must sum the values stored in 8 independent linked lists, each containing 125,000 nodes.

The baseline finishes one list before moving to the next. That creates one long chain of dependent cache misses, so the CPU often sits idle waiting for memory.

Change the traversal order so misses from different lists can overlap and the core can exploit more memory-level parallelism.
prompt: Write `long solve(Node **heads, int num_lists)` to visit every node exactly once and return the total sum, while interleaving work across lists to expose independent memory misses.
expectedOutput: Return one 64-bit integer equal to the sum of all node values across all input lists.
constraints: Input is delivered as 8 linked-list heads
You must process every node exactly once
You may change traversal order across lists

examples.input: heads[8] where each head points to a 125K-node list
examples.explanation: Advancing several lists in round-robin fashion exposes multiple independent miss streams instead of only one.

title: Bottleneck Triage — Diagnose and Fix
description:
This workload is slow for several independent reasons.

Baseline metrics:
• IPC: 0.7  (target: > 3.0)
• L1 MPKI: 36.0  (target: < 4.0)
• Branch MPKI: 18.0  (target: < 2.0)

The starter code combines three different bottlenecks: poor locality, an unpredictable branch, and unnecessary dependency pressure. Use the counters, source, and assembly to identify those issues and rewrite the loop so all targets are met at the same time.
prompt: Rewrite `long solve(int *arr, int n)` so it returns the correct total while fixing the branch, cache-locality, and dependency problems in the baseline.
expectedOutput: Return the exact reference total and satisfy every published performance target in the same run.
constraints: Output must match the reference total
All three targets must be met simultaneously
You may change traversal order and control flow

title: Strided Sum — Hide Latency with Prefetch
description:
You must sum one integer from every 64-byte region of a large array.

The baseline reads `arr[i * 16]`, so each iteration pulls from a new cache line. That pattern easily turns into a latency-bound loop if the core waits for one miss at a time.

Use techniques such as software prefetching, unrolling, or multiple accumulators so several memory accesses can be in flight together.
prompt: Write `long solve(int *arr, int n)` to return the sum of `arr[i * 16]` for `i = 0..n-1`, while restructuring the loop to expose more memory-level parallelism.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum of the stride-16 stream.
constraints: Input allocation contains at least n * 16 integers
You must read arr[i * 16] exactly once per i

examples.explanation: Prefetching future cache lines and keeping several accumulators live helps overlap independent misses.

title: Bitset Scan — Turn Scalar Loops into Throughput
description:
You must count all set bits in a large bitmap.

The baseline examines all 64 bit positions of every word with a scalar inner loop. That wastes instructions and underuses the CPU's dedicated population-count hardware.

Replace the bit-by-bit scan with a throughput-friendly approach that maps well to popcount instructions.
prompt: Write `unsigned long long solve(unsigned long long *bits, int words)` to return the total number of set bits across `words` 64-bit words.
expectedOutput: Return the exact population count as an unsigned 64-bit integer.
constraints: Compiler builtins such as __builtin_popcountll are allowed

examples.explanation: A dedicated popcount operation replaces 64 scalar shifts and masks per word.

title: Particle Score — Repack Structs for Bandwidth
description:
Each particle stores four float fields in an array-of-structs layout. The computation only needs the expression `x*w + y*z` for every particle, but the baseline processes the array in a way that leaves bandwidth and instruction throughput on the table.

Repack the hot fields into a denser layout, or otherwise restructure the loop, so the CPU can stream data and arithmetic more efficiently.
prompt: Write `float solve(Particle *p, int n)` to return `sum(p[i].x * p[i].w + p[i].y * p[i].z)` for all `n` particles.
expectedOutput: Return the floating-point total within an absolute tolerance of 1e-4.
constraints: Do not modify the particle values

examples.input: Particle {x, y, z, w} repeated 200K times
examples.explanation: Copying hot fields into dense arrays can reduce wasted bandwidth and expose cleaner inner loops.

title: Image Blur — Tile the Working Set
description:
Apply a horizontal 3-tap blur to a 512×512 image.

The arithmetic per pixel is small, so performance depends mostly on keeping rows hot in cache and writing the output sequentially.

Rewrite the starter code with pointer arithmetic, tiling, unrolling, or similar loop improvements so the working set stays cache-friendly.
prompt: Write `void solve(float *in, float *out, int width, int height)` so each non-edge output pixel is the average of its left, center, and right neighbors, while edge pixels are copied unchanged.
expectedOutput: The checksum of the output image must match the reference within an absolute tolerance of 1e-4.
constraints: Edge pixels must be copied without modification

examples.explanation: Tiling by rows or blocks helps the CPU reuse nearby pixels and write outputs sequentially.

title: Score Window — Remove Unpredictable Branches
description:
A scoring loop must add only the values inside a target range.

The baseline uses two nested branches per element. When the input scores are spread roughly uniformly, those branches become hard to predict and hurt front-end throughput.

Rewrite the loop so the result stays exact but the hot path becomes much more predictable, ideally branchless.
prompt: Write `long solve(int *scores, int n)` to return the sum of every `scores[i]` in the inclusive range [50, 200].
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum of all scores inside the window.
constraints: scores[i] are integers in the range 0..255

examples.explanation: Branchless range checks keep the hot loop predictable even when valid scores are not clustered.

title: ECE Lab — 2D Jacobi Stencil Cache Blocking
description:
This challenge mirrors a classic cache-optimization lab from upper-level computer architecture courses.

You must perform one Jacobi sweep on a 1024×1024 grid. The baseline is correct, but it streams through a large 2D array with limited attention to cache reuse in the hot loop.

Rewrite the kernel so it produces the same numerical result while improving locality in L1 and L2. Row blocking, pointer hoisting, and light unrolling are all valid approaches.
prompt: Write `void solve(const float *in, float *out, int n)` to compute one 5-point Jacobi update on an `n × n` row-major grid. Copy boundary cells unchanged, and set each interior cell to `0.5*center + 0.125*(north + south + west + east)` without changing the final checksum.
expectedOutput: The harness prints a single floating-point checksum of the output grid. Your result must match the reference within an absolute tolerance of 1e-4.
constraints: Boundary cells must be copied exactly from the input
Interior update formula must remain numerically equivalent

examples.explanation: The optimization target is not a different algorithm. You are improving loop structure and locality while preserving the exact stencil semantics.

title: Irregular Gather — Prefetch Ahead of Random Access
description:
Sum 128K integers accessed in a random order defined by an index permutation.

The baseline walks `indices[]` sequentially and fetches `data[indices[i]]` on demand. Because each index points to a random location in a 512 KB data array, every iteration triggers an L1 miss — and the CPU stalls waiting for each one before it can compute the next address.

Add software prefetch hints so the CPU requests the next cache line before it is needed, allowing misses to overlap with useful work.

The key metric is L1D average miss latency. On the baseline it will be 45–55 cycles because the CPU sits idle. With effective prefetching it should drop below 25 cycles as future accesses are already in flight.
prompt: Write `long solve(const int *data, const int *indices, int n)` to return the sum of `data[indices[i]]` for all `i`, using `__builtin_prefetch` to hide the latency of random memory accesses.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum of all gathered values.
constraints: indices[] is a permutation of 0..n-1 — every element accessed exactly once
__builtin_prefetch is allowed and required to meet targets

examples.input: data[128K] of random ints 1..256, indices[128K] = random permutation
examples.explanation: __builtin_prefetch(&data[indices[i + D]], 0, 1) with distance D=16–32 tells the CPU to fetch the cache line D iterations ahead, so it arrives before the load instruction needs it.

title: Histogram — Break Write Dependency Chains
description:
Fill a 256-bucket histogram from 2 million random bytes.

The baseline does `hist[arr[i]]++` on every element. When two consecutive elements share the same bucket, the second increment must wait for the first to complete — a write-after-write dependency chain that stalls the pipeline.

Break those chains by computing several independent partial histograms in parallel and merging them at the end. With 4 interleaved histograms, the probability that two consecutive updates collide on the same bucket drops dramatically, so the CPU can retire multiple updates per cycle.
prompt: Write `void solve(const unsigned char *arr, int n, unsigned int *hist)` to count occurrences of each byte value 0–255, with hist[] zeroed on entry, using interleaved partial histograms to reduce write dependency stalls.
expectedOutput: hist[i] must equal the exact count of byte value i in arr[].
constraints: hist[] is zeroed before your function is called
hist[i] must match the reference count exactly

examples.input: arr[2M] of random bytes 0–255, hist[256] zeroed
examples.output: hist[i] = count of value i in arr
examples.explanation: Four interleaved histograms h0–h3 each accumulate every 4th element. Any two consecutive updates go to different histograms, eliminating write-after-write stalls.

title: 3D Array — Fix Loop Order for Sequential Access
description:
Sum all elements of a 64×64×64 integer array.

The array is stored in row-major order: element `[i][j][k]` lives at offset `i*64*64 + j*64 + k`. When k varies fastest in the inner loop, consecutive accesses are adjacent in memory — one cache line covers 16 integers.

The baseline iterates with i in the inner loop instead, so each step jumps by 64×64 = 4096 integers (16 KB), pulling a new cache line on every iteration.

Simply reorder the three loops so k varies fastest. This turns 4096-element strides into unit strides and converts almost every L1 miss into a hit.
prompt: Write `long solve(int *arr, int n)` to return the sum of all `n×n×n` integers stored row-major in `arr`, with the innermost loop iterating over the last (k) dimension.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum of all n³ elements.
constraints: arr is row-major: element [i][j][k] is at arr[i*n*n + j*n + k]

examples.explanation: Outer i, middle j, inner k → arr[i*n*n + j*n + k] increments by 1 per inner step. The bad version has i innermost → stride n*n = 4096 per step.

title: Binary Search — Cache-Friendly Eytzinger Layout
description:
Search for 100,000 query values in a sorted array of 65,536 keys.

Standard binary search touches O(log₂ N) ≈ 16 cache lines per query, one per level. Each miss is serial — the next address is unknown until the current comparison resolves. With 100K queries that is ~1.6 million sequentially dependent cache misses.

The Eytzinger layout stores the binary search tree in BFS order: the root at index 1, its children at 2 and 3, and so on. Children of node k are at 2k and 2k+1. This makes the next two levels addressable before the current comparison finishes, enabling prefetch hints that hide 2 levels of latency per step.

Rearrange the keys into Eytzinger order and use `__builtin_prefetch` to overlap cache misses with computation.
prompt: Write `int solve(const int *keys, int n, const int *queries, int q)` to return the count of queries found in the key set. You may rearrange keys internally before searching.
expectedOutput: Return the exact integer count of queries that exist in the key array.
constraints: keys[] is sorted ascending with n distinct values (≤65536)
Return exact count of found queries

examples.output: count of queries present in keys
examples.explanation: Eytzinger build: eyt[1]=median, eyt[2]=left-median, eyt[3]=right-median recursively. Search: k=1; while(k<=n) { prefetch eyt[4k]; k=2k+(eyt[k]<target); }

title: Streaming Computation — Multiple Accumulators for ILP
description:
Compute `sum((src[i] * src[i]) & 0xFFFF)` for 1 million bytes.

The baseline uses a single running accumulator, so every addition must wait for the previous one to complete — a serial dependency chain that limits the CPU to one add per cycle regardless of how wide the execution units are.

Unroll the loop and use multiple independent accumulators so the out-of-order core can issue several multiply-and-mask operations simultaneously. The computation is entirely ALU-bound with no cache misses — this is a pure ILP exercise that shows how dependency chains limit throughput even on modern CPUs.
prompt: Write `long solve(const unsigned char *src, int n)` to return `sum((src[i] * src[i]) & 0xFFFF)` using multiple independent accumulators to exploit instruction-level parallelism.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum.

examples.explanation: Four accumulators s0,s1,s2,s3 each handle every 4th element independently. The CPU can compute all four multiply-and-mask operations in parallel since they share no data dependencies.

title: 2D Grid Sum — Fix Column-First Access Order
description:
Sum all values in a large row-major 2D grid.

The baseline walks the grid column-first: the outer loop steps across columns (x), and the inner loop steps down rows (y). Because the array is stored in row-major order, consecutive iterations of the inner loop jump by an entire row width — a stride of 2048 integers, or 8 KB. Every step lands on a cold cache line, so the inner loop is almost always waiting for memory.

Rewrite the traversal so the inner loop moves along a single row (x varies fastest). Consecutive accesses are then adjacent in memory, one cache line covers 16 elements, and the L1 hit rate improves dramatically. Tiled blocking can push performance further, but even a simple loop-order swap already meets all targets.
prompt: Write `long solve(int *grid, int n)` to return the exact sum of all values in an `n × n` row-major integer grid, traversing memory in a cache-friendly order.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum of all grid elements.
constraints: grid is stored row-major: element [y][x] is at grid[y*n + x]

examples.explanation: Outer y, inner x → grid[y*n+x] increments by 1 per inner step. The bad version has x outer, y inner → stride n=2048 ints (8 KB) per step, guaranteeing an L1 miss every iteration.

title: SAXPY — Unlock Auto-Vectorization
description:
Compute the classic SAXPY update `y[i] = a*x[i] + y[i]` over a large float array.

The baseline is correct but intentionally conservative. Rewrite the loop into a regular, vectorization-friendly form so the compiler and the out-of-order core can extract more throughput.

This is a practical bridge from ILP thinking to SIMD-style optimization, even without explicit intrinsics.
prompt: Write `void solve(float a, const float *x, float *y, int n)` to update all `n` elements of `y` with `a*x[i] + y[i]`.
expectedOutput: The harness prints a checksum of the updated y array. Your result must match the reference within an absolute tolerance of 1e-4.

examples.explanation: Simple contiguous loops with no aliasing surprises are ideal auto-vectorization targets.

title: Gather Reordering — Cluster Accesses by Cache Region
description:
Sum integers from a large array using an index permutation.

The baseline walks the permutation in arrival order, so each iteration may jump to a completely different region of the data array. With a 512 KB data array and indices scattered randomly, most accesses land on cold cache lines, and the CPU stalls waiting for memory on nearly every iteration.

Reorder the accesses internally so indices that point to the same cache-line region are processed together. By sorting or bucketing indices before gathering, you turn a random-access stream into a set of short sequential bursts, allowing the hardware prefetcher to help and dramatically reducing the number of distinct cache lines touched at any moment. You must still read every referenced element exactly once and return the exact total.
prompt: Write `long solve(const int *data, const int *indices, int n)` to return the exact sum of `data[indices[i]]` for all `i`, while improving cache locality by regrouping accesses before gathering.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit sum of all gathered values.
constraints: You must access every referenced element exactly once

examples.explanation: Grouping indices that fall within the same cache-line or page region reduces the number of distinct cold lines touched and lets the hardware prefetcher cover short sequential runs.

title: Masked SAXPY — Remove Branches, Unlock Throughput
description:
Apply a masked SAXPY update: if `mask[i]` is 1, do `y[i] = a*x[i] + y[i]`; otherwise leave `y[i]` unchanged.

The baseline uses a branch on every element. With a roughly 50/50 mask, that branch is hard to predict and also makes the hot loop less friendly to vectorization.

Rewrite the loop so it stays exact but becomes branchless and throughput-oriented.
prompt: Write `void solve(float a, const float *x, float *y, const unsigned char *mask, int n)` to apply the masked SAXPY update exactly.
expectedOutput: The harness prints a checksum of y. Your result must match the reference within an absolute tolerance of 1e-4.

examples.explanation: A branchless multiply-by-mask form keeps the loop regular and predictable.

title: Dot Product — Eight Accumulators for ILP
description:
Compute the dot product of two large float arrays.

The baseline uses one running accumulator, which creates a long floating-point dependency chain. That limits instruction-level parallelism even when data is already streaming nicely from memory.

Break the chain with several independent partial sums, then combine them at the end.
prompt: Write `float solve(const float *a, const float *b, int n)` to return the dot product of two float arrays while exposing more ILP than a single-accumulator loop.
expectedOutput: Return a floating-point result that matches the reference within an absolute tolerance of 1e-3.

examples.explanation: Independent accumulators let the out-of-order core overlap more multiply-add work.

title: Grade Bands — Replace Nested Branches with a LUT
description:
Classify scores into grade bands over many repeated passes.

The baseline uses a nested if/else tree for every score on every pass. With scores spread broadly across the input range, the control flow is less predictable than it needs to be.

Precompute a tiny lookup table once, then turn the hot loop into a simple table lookup and accumulation.
prompt: Write `long solve(const unsigned char *scores, int n)` to return the weighted total across 200 passes, where scores map to weights by band.
expectedOutput: Return the exact 64-bit total produced by the reference classification logic over all 200 passes.

examples.output: sum of band weights over all passes
examples.explanation: A 101-entry or 256-entry lookup table removes nested branches from the repeated hot loop.
